title: Leader of Jewish Greens calls for Zack Polanski to resign
summary: Vivien Lichtenstein says party leader should stand down over ‘Zionism is racism’ policy after losing byelection

blocks.text: The leader of the Jewish Greens has called for Zack Polanski to step down as pressure increases on the Green leader to acknowledge anger within the party over a new policy which equates Zionism with racism and calls for the state of Israel to be abolished.

The comments by Vivien Lichtenstein come after Caroline Lucas, the Greens’ former leader and first MP, criticised Polanski for a lack of leadership in missing the debate and vote at the weekend which resulted in the policy being passed.

Lichtenstein had warned she was considering quitting the Green party of England and Wales in the wake of the vote at the party conference to adopt the policy, which states that Zionism is racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state.
Polanski was not at the conference on Sunday when the motion was debated; instead he was campaigning for Holborn and St Pancras byelection, in which he finished second to Labour.

In post-byelection interviews, Polanski said he would have voted against the motion had he attended. Two amendments he supported, including one that called for a two-state solution rather than a single Palestinian state, were voted down.

Speaking to Times Radio, Lichtenstein said that even though Polanski was campaigning, he should have spoken and voted for the amendments online, which was an option. “He should have done that. And I think that was a big mistake on his part.”

Lichtenstein said she was surprised to hear Polanski say he had been working with Jewish members of the party, adding: “I don’t know which Jewish members of the party he’s been working with. It certainly hasn’t been with the Jewish Greens committee.”
Asked if he should continue in his role, she replied: “No, I think he should resign.”
Speaking to Newsnight on Thursday, before the byelection result, Lucas, who remains one of the Greens’ best-known and popular figures, said Polanski “should have been there and he should have voted”.

She went on: “I would have hoped that he would have really been a very strong critic of this motion, because the motion was flawed from top to bottom in my view. It’s dangerous, it’s divisive, it tries to have a singular definition of Zionism when we know that there are many.”
Asked if Polansksi should stand down, Lucas did not definitively say he should remain as leader: “I think let’s just see what happens in the… coming days and weeks.

“Obviously he has been completely taken up with this byelection. I want him to speak now about what’s happened. I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday. I think the jury is out about whether or not he will do that, but I very much hope he will. But that is a long way from full-throated support.”
Jonathan Bartley, who was formerly the Green co-leader with Lucas, and is now a councillor in Lambeth, south London, called on Polanski to “put his hands up” and apologise.
“I think [the policy vote] was a failure of leadership from Zack and there is a certain toxicity now from the Green party,” he told the BBC.

There is no formal mechanism for ejecting a leader of the Greens. However, they are re-elected every two years, meaning Polanski, who took over in September 2025, will have to go before party members again in less than a year.
